articles.title: ET 40 Under 40: Meet India's 40 young leaders
articles.summary: The Economic Times 40 under Forty returns for its 12th edition with a cohort that reflects just how much the idea of leadership has changed over the years. The 40 honorees for 2026 come from a wide range of fields—business, finance and professional services to technology, law, social impact, art, culture and sports—and offer a broader view of the people shaping the country’s next chapter.The diversity of the cohort is striking, highlighting the many paths young professionals are taking toward success and leadership. Some are building businesses from the ground up while others are steering family enterprises into new territories. There are investors deploying capital, professionals leading organisations through change, innovators creating new products and ideas, and individuals influencing India’s legal, social and cultural landscape.Financial services, venture capital and private equity have the highest representation this year, accounting for 17.5% of the list, with seven honorees, while those from professional services (5) account for 12.5%. Owner professionals; consumer and luxury; technology, media, telecom and legal services contribute four (10%) honorees each. Three achievers (7.5%) from the industrial sector and another two (5%) from the social sector add to the eclectic mix. Two (5%) global Indians feature on the list as well, underscoring the reach of the country's talent across geographies.134029366The inclusion of five people (12.5%) from art, culture and sports is particularly significant. It recognises that some of India’s most influential voices are building their impact through creativity, cultural influence, grit, determination and on-ground performance. Women make up 11 of this year’s 40 honorees, representing 27.5% of the cohort, marking their highest representation in the list since the seventh edition.134029416Over the years, The Economic Times 40 under Forty has evolved into an important marker of young talent across India’s changing economy. The class of 2026 adds another 40 names to an alumni base that numbers 440, many of whom have gone on to shape businesses and institutions.134029559METHODOLOGYThe Economic Times has compiled its list of India’s top 40 leaders under forty — a celebration of the country’s most dynamic and promising talent — for the 12th year. The process began with the formation of a distinguished jury tasked with identifying India’s next generation of leaders.134029598Nominations were invited through multiple channels: self and corporate nominations; recommendations from the 440-strong ET 40 Under Forty alumni network; and inputs from leading executive search firms such as Accord and EMA Partners, among others, as well as the ET Leadership team. Together, these efforts yielded an extensive pool of over 650 nominations.134029628The preliminary list featured a diverse mix of professionals, entrepreneurs and owner-promoters across industries. A rigorous multi-stage evaluation followed. Team ET conducted the first round of screening, shortlisting 250 profiles based on scale, impact, innovation and value creation. articles.title: UK chaos: Flights resume but delays ahead
articles.summary: Flights resumed at major UK airports on Wednesday after an air traffic control system failure cancelled more than 1,000 flights and caused delays across Britain. Heathrow and Gatwick warned that disruption could continue as airlines reposition aircraft and crew.Britain’s National Air Traffic Services (NATS) said it had resolved the problem in its flight processing system on Tuesday evening. However, delays continued across 15 UK airports and beyond as airlines and airports worked to clear a backlog of flights.Heathrow resumed departures but suspended arrivals for the rest of Tuesday night. The airport said flights were operating today, but warned that some disruption may continue.Gatwick also said its operations would take time to return to normal.“We still anticipate that it will take time for our operations to fully return to normal,” the airport said.Passengers were left stranded on aircraft, at terminals and at baggage collection areas during the disruption.British Airways cancelled or diverted more than 100 flights. The airline said aircraft and crew had ended up in different locations, affecting its operations.“The severity of the issue means there will be a significant knock-on impact,” a British Airways spokesperson said. “This incident was entirely out of our control and incredibly frustrating for our customers and colleagues, with aircraft and crews ending up out of place.”Passengers on a British Airways flight scheduled to fly from Heathrow to Baltimore spent four hours on the ground before leaving the aircraft. Cabin crew served pasta and chicken curry during the delay, while some passengers watched films or walked through the aisles.Passengers later reported confusion at the baggage claim area and said they were told to file claims for their bags.At Gatwick, Josie Donoghue spent three hours on a plane before her Ryanair flight to Ireland was cancelled.“Getting through that airport was like trying to get out of Alcatraz,” she said, referring to the former island prison in San Francisco Bay. “It’s just an absolute nightmare down there. It’s the only word I can use to describe it.”Ryanair said more than 65,000 passengers were affected and that it had cancelled more than 50 scheduled flights.EasyJet said some of its flights were “unable to operate” and that the system failure caused “delays to flights across Europe.”Other affected airports included London Stansted and London City, as well as airports in Manchester, Birmingham and Scotland. Passengers have been advised to check their flight status with their airline before travelling.
